newsitem.title: USA: New York's tax-free clothing week - big deals or big deal?.
newsitem.headline: New York's tax-free clothing week - big deals or big deal?.

text.p: It's no secret that many New Yorkers head over the border to New Jersey to shop since there's no sales tax on most clothes in the Garden State.

Many take bridges and tunnels and trains to escape New York City's 8.25 percent tax on coats, dresses or pants. The Empire State estimates that it looses about $700 million a year from such cross-border shoppers.

But now it's pay-back time. New York is fighting fire with fire. A one-week moratorium on sales tax on most clothing began Jan. 18 and will run for one week. New York City and State have decided to make shopping trips to the 'burbs in New Jersey, Pennsylvania or Connecticut not worth the car fare.

The state for the week lifted its 4 percent sales tax and all but seven of New York's 62 counties ditched local taxes on clothes, keeping most state residents from paying tax on any item under $500. The state's Metropolitan Transportation Authority also decided to put on hold its 0.25 percent tax for the week.

New Yorkers pay varying sales taxes across the state, depending on local tax rates. Nassau County, on suburban Long Island, has the state's highest sales tax of 8.50 percent while Delaware County, on the state's Southern Tier, has the lowest with 6 percent.

For New York State retailers January is a rather slow month. It's hard to get terribly excited about annual white sales for bedding and other housewares. In terms of clothing, there are deep discounts all over town, but the wares are looking kind of shop-worn about now.
What better time to bring in some excitement. Actually, state officials originally wanted to have the tax-free week in December, but it was decided the loss to the state would have been too great.

So rather than omit sales tax during the busiest time of the year, the experiment was put off until this week, risking $20 million in tax revenue to determine how much the tax really harms retailers, New York officials said.
State and local spokesmen drew a blank when asked if other states had ever had a sales tax suspension like New York's.
Is it paying off?

While it's just mid-week, retailers can't give a final tally as to whether people are buying. The New York City Department of Finance doesn't expect any definitive reports from retailers for a few months.

But from all appearances, shoppers are indeed coming in, at least to browse. Not only are retailers marking down clothes from 20 percent to 75 percent to clear the racks for spring fashions, but the suspension of sales tax appears to be the final sweetener.
At Today's Man in Manhattan, store officials said sales were up 250 percent over the same week last year, keeping in mind that last year's January was one non-stop snow storm.
"I expected a huge increase, but I didn't expect it to be as good as it was," store manager Greg Cabral said.
As a customer said at Forman's of Orchard Street, a discounter of women's clothing, "I wouldn't be buying the Austin Reed outfit if it wasn't for no tax."
At Loehmann's in Lake Success, N.Y., on Long Island, sales associates remarked that they had never seen so many shoppers on a Sunday. The line for the cashier was several minutes long.

"It is long overdue," Walter Eisenhardt, store manager of Barneys New York in the World Financial Centre, said. "It is giving New Yorkers the opportunity to enjoy the same tax-free purchases as someone in New Jersey has been able to enjoy all these years."
While only five states have no sales tax on clothing, a number have some exemptions on work clothes or childrens clothes, according to the Commerce Clearing House, a publisher of detailed tax data.
The tax free states are: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon.
Seven states exempt clothing sales depending on value, use, materials or expected life of the garment -- Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Texas.
California and Idaho exempt clothing sold to nonprofit groups that distribute the items free to school children. If the clothing is going to be used in a display, it's tax-free in Washington.
But the question remains for New Yorkers, after the tax-free shopping spree, will some shoppers once again escape from New York?

"While New York will do no tax on clothing for one week, New Jersey for 52 weeks out of the year has no tax on clothing, drugs, utilities or fuel and food, among several other items," Lisa Kruse, spokeswoman for the New Jersey Department of Commerce, said. "We think shoppers will remember who is tax free all year long."
However, most New York City residents shop at local stores since they find it inconvenient to spend a big part of the day in the car to save 8 percent.

Yet the seed has been sown. New York Gov. George Pataki said on Tuesday that while it would be hard to eliminate the 4 percent state sales tax on clothing this year, he would back gradually eliminating the tax.
